buddhist_raga.name: Inflame lust and passion in the beholder
buddhist_raga.notes: As the personification of Passion/Attachment, she works the sensual lure against the meditator, the most basic distraction from the path.

sources.reference: Saṃyutta Nikāya, Dhītaro-sutta (SN 4.25)

buddhist_tanha.name: Rouse craving and unquenchable thirst
buddhist_tanha.notes: Eldest daughter of Māra, the jealous thirst for pleasure, existence and recognition that can never be satisfied; she leads the trio's attempt to seduce the Buddha.

sources.reference: Saṃyutta Nikāya, Dhītaro-sutta (SN 4.25)

buddhist_virudhaka.name: Cut through ignorance with the sword of wisdom
buddhist_virudhaka.notes: His blade symbolises the wisdom that severs ignorance and quickens the roots of virtue ('Increase and Growth', the meaning of his name).

sources.reference: Four Heavenly Kings (Lokapāla) iconographic tradition; Cleveland Museum of Art Virudhaka relief

buddhist_virupaksa.name: See all things across the world with far-seeing eyes
buddhist_virupaksa.notes: His name 'He of Misshapen/Broad Eyes' (Ch. 廣目, 'Broad Eye') marks his power to survey the world; his glance is said to be harmful, so he averts it to the stūpa he carries.

sources.reference: Four Heavenly Kings (Lokapāla) iconographic tradition

bunyoro_ndahura.name: Conquer and reorganise the realm of Kitara
bunyoro_ndahura.notes: First fully realised Bacwezi ruler; remembered as the warrior who slew the usurper Bukuku and extended Kitara across Ankole, Buganda, Toro and Busoga.

sources.reference: Bunyoro-Kitara oral tradition of the Bacwezi dynasty

bunyoro_ndahura.name: Send and lift epidemic smallpox
bunyoro_ndahura.notes: Venerated as Ndahura Atwooki, the embandwa spirit of smallpox and epidemics in the Kubandwa cult.

sources.reference: Kubandwa (Cwezi) possession-cult tradition, interlacustrine Uganda

buganda_wanema.name: Father the great lubaale of the lake and of war
buganda_wanema.notes: Ssese-island progenitor; father of Mukasa the lake-god, Kibuka the war-god, Musisi and Wamala, the lineage from which the principal Baganda gods came to the mainland.

sources.reference: New Vision, 'Ssese Islands: the wealthy store for Buganda traditions'; Roscoe, The Baganda (1911)

buganda_wanema.name: Afflict and heal lameness and physical handicap
buganda_wanema.notes: His name is connected with lameness; his Ssese shrine (Bukasa Island) was resorted to over crippling and bodily handicap.

sources.reference: Baganda balubaale tradition; Roscoe, The Baganda (1911)

buganda_katonda.name: Judge mortals as the eternal king of the universe
buganda_katonda.notes: Revered as father of the gods, the ever-present one and ultimate judge, standing above the balubaale.

sources.reference: Roscoe, The Baganda (1911); Baganda traditional invocations to Katonda

buganda_kawumpuli.name: Send and withhold epidemic plague
buganda_kawumpuli.notes: Lubaale of plague among the balubaale; his medium was consulted to send or stay outbreaks of pestilence.

sources.reference: Roscoe, The Baganda (1911); Kawumpuli plague-shrine tradition

burmese_me_wunna.name: Live on the flowers of Mount Popa
burmese_me_wunna.notes: The flower-eating ogress (belu) of Popa, whose appetite for the mountain's blossoms marks her as its indwelling mother-spirit.

sources.reference: Popa Medaw / Me Wunna nat tradition, Mount Popa

buganda_kintu.name: Vanish without dying into the Magonga forest
buganda_kintu.notes: Unlike later kabakas Kintu is said not to have died but to have disappeared into the forest at Magonga (Buddu); his hidden presence there underpins his standing as undying progenitor.

sources.reference: Kintu cycle, Buganda; Magonga (Bukunja) tradition

buddhist_vaishravana.name: Treasure stūpa (pagoda)
buddhist_vaishravana.notes: Reliquary pagoda held in one hand, storing immeasurable wealth; emblem of his role as wealth-giver (Kubera).

sources.reference: Bishamonten / Tamonten iconographic tradition (Buddhistdoor, 'King of Kings')

buddhist_vaishravana.name: Halberd (war-spear)
buddhist_vaishravana.notes: Three-pronged spear or baton borne in the other hand, marking him as fierce guardian of the north.

sources.reference: Four Heavenly Kings (Lokapāla) iconographic tradition

buddhist_virudhaka.name: Warrior armour
buddhist_virudhaka.notes: Blue-faced king depicted in full armour beneath his upraised sword.

sources.reference: Four Heavenly Kings (Lokapāla) iconographic tradition; Cleveland Museum of Art 1918.544

buganda_walumbe.name: The Ttanda pits near Mityana
buganda_walumbe.notes: The roughly 240 deep pits at Ttanda, dug as Walumbe fled underground from Kayikuuzi; venerated as shrines where visitors go barefoot.

sources.reference: Ttanda pits of Buganda; Daily Monitor, 'Tanda pits: the legend of Walumbe'

buganda_mukasa.name: Conical reed temple on Bubembe Island
buganda_mukasa.notes: Conical reed shrine on Bubembe, the chief temple of the lake-god, served by a secluded female medium (mandwa) and priest.

sources.reference: Roscoe, The Baganda (1911); Bubembe Island temple tradition

buganda_kibuka.name: Jawbone relic of Kibuka
buganda_kibuka.notes: His jawbone, kept in the fireproof inner chamber at Mbaale; embodied the god's presence and was consulted as oracle. Taken to Cambridge by Roscoe, repatriated to the Uganda Museum in 1961.

sources.reference: Roscoe, The Baganda (1911); Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, Cambridge / Uganda Museum repatriation records

buganda_kibuka.name: Shield Liigyamirembe and war-spear
buganda_kibuka.notes: Among Kibuka's regalia at the Mbaale shrine, integrated by the kabaka into coronation ritual; with a stool spread with lion or leopard skin.

sources.reference: Kibuka shrine relics, Mbaale (Gods' Collections case study)

buryat_erlen_khan.name: Black iron sword and shield
buryat_erlen_khan.notes: Black-iron arms of the lord of the lower world, who dwells in an underground iron palace.

sources.reference: Turkic-Mongolic Erlik tradition (Siberian/Buryat shamanism)

buganda_kintu.name: Shrine of Kintu at Magonga
buganda_kintu.notes: Sacred site in the Magonga (Bukunja) forest where the undying first man is held to have vanished; a focus of veneration tying the living kabaka lineage to its progenitor.

sources.reference: Kintu cycle, Buganda; Magonga forest tradition

bunyoro_wamara.name: Lake Wamala
bunyoro_wamara.notes: The lake into which the last Bacwezi king is said to have vanished; it bears his name and is a centre of Kubandwa veneration.

sources.reference: Bacwezi disappearance traditions, interlacustrine Uganda

burmese_thagyamin.gloss: Lord Sakka, King of the Nats (from Skt. Śakra)

sources.reference: Ugaritic epithet hyn of Kothar; Smith, Ugaritic Baal Cycle

sources.reference: Popa Medaw / Mount Popa nat tradition

buganda_mukasa.name: Annual royal offering at Bubembe
buganda_mukasa.notes: The kabaka sent yearly an offering of cattle with a petition for prosperity and good harvests to the Bubembe temple; the secluded medium (mandwa) delivered the god's oracles. Mukasa was a kindly lubaale who never demanded human sacrifice.

sources.reference: Roscoe, The Baganda (1911); Bubembe Island temple tradition

buganda_kibuka.name: War oracle at the Mbaale shrine
buganda_kibuka.notes: Before campaigns the kabaka consulted Kibuka through the medium at Mbaale; his relics and regalia were carried in war and woven into the coronation rite as national war-god.

sources.reference: Roscoe, The Baganda (1911); Kibuka shrine relics tradition

buganda_katonda.name: Temples of Katonda in Kyagwe
buganda_katonda.notes: Three temples in Kyagwe tended by priests of the Njovu (Elephant) clan; daily morning invocations called on Katonda Ssewannaku for protection and prosperity.

sources.reference: Roscoe, The Baganda (1911); Katonda temple tradition

bunyoro_ndahura.name: Kubandwa possession of the Ndahura spirit
bunyoro_ndahura.notes: Mediums (embandwa) become possessed by Ndahura, the Bacwezi spirit of smallpox and epidemics; Mubende Hill, linked with Ndahura and his mother Nakayima, is a major pilgrimage site for healing and fertility.

sources.reference: Kubandwa (Cwezi) cult tradition; Mubende Hill / Nakayima site

bunyoro_wamara.name: Kubandwa veneration of Wamara
bunyoro_wamara.notes: Chief among the embandwa spirits venerated after the Bacwezi vanished; associated with rain and rivers and with Lake Wamala, which bears his name.

sources.reference: Kubandwa (Cwezi) cult tradition, interlacustrine Uganda

burmese_thagyamin.name: Thingyan (Burmese New Year water festival)
burmese_thagyamin.notes: At the new year Thagyamin descends to the human world to record the deeds of mortals — the virtuous in a golden book, the wicked in a book of dog-skin — his arrival marking the start of Thingyan.

sources.reference: Thagyamin / Thingyan tradition, Burma

burmese_shwe_hpyin_naungdaw.name: Taungbyon Nat Festival
burmese_shwe_hpyin_naungdaw.notes: The largest nat festival in Myanmar, held over six days at Taungbyon village near Mandalay for the Shwe Hpyin brothers; spirit-mediums (nat-kadaw) dance to the hsaing waing orchestra and receive offerings of money, flowers and liquor. Devotees avoid pork in honour of their father Byatta.

sources.reference: Taungbyone Festival tradition, Mandalay

burmese_shwe_hpyin_nyidaw.name: Taungbyon Nat Festival
burmese_shwe_hpyin_nyidaw.notes: Worshipped with his elder brother at the six-day Taungbyon festival; the younger brother receives liquor, tobacco and revelry from devotees through possessed mediums.

sources.reference: Taungbyone Festival tradition, Mandalay

burmese_min_mahagiri.name: Household nat of the house-post
burmese_min_mahagiri.notes: Official household nat venerated through a dressed coconut hung on the main house-post, replaced when the stem withers; enshrined with his sister at the Tharabha Gate of Bagan and on Mount Popa.

sources.reference: Mahagiri household-nat tradition, Burma

canaanite_baal.name: Sacrifice to Baal of Zaphon
canaanite_baal.notes: Animal sacrifice on stone altars formed the core of his cult; bulls were the premier offering for the 'Bull of Ugarit', though sheep and goats served regular rites.

sources.reference: Ugaritic ritual texts; Baal cult at Ugarit

canaanite_anat.name: Animal offerings to Anat
canaanite_anat.notes: Prominent in the Ugaritic cult, with offerings of rams and bulls and many votive inscriptions; named frequently in deity and offering lists.

sources.reference: Ugaritic offering and deity lists; votive inscriptions to Anat

burmese_me_wunna.name: Pilgrimage to Popa Medaw on Mount Popa
burmese_me_wunna.notes: As Popa Medaw, the 'Royal Mother of Popa', she is venerated at the Taungkalat shrine of the Thirty-Seven Nats; pilgrims bring flowers, coconuts and bananas, especially at the Nayon (May–June) and Nadaw (November–December) full-moon festivals.

sources.reference: Mount Popa / Taungkalat nat-shrine tradition

burmese_byatta.name: Veneration of Byatta on Mount Popa
burmese_byatta.notes: The deified royal flower-gatherer is honoured among the nats of Mount Popa beside his consort Popa Medaw and at the Taungbyon festival as father of the Shwe Hpyin brothers.

sources.reference: Mount Popa nat tradition; Taungbyone festival

buganda_kawumpuli.name: Plague shrine of Kawumpuli
buganda_kawumpuli.notes: Shrine at Buyego in Bulemeezi (Luwero area) where the plague-lubaale was propitiated, especially in time of pestilence.

sources.reference: Roscoe, The Baganda (1911); Kawumpuli plague-shrine tradition

buryat_geser.name: Tailgan offering to the heaven-sent hero
buryat_geser.notes: Geser of the Abai Geser epic is invoked in Buryat tailgan rites alongside the western tengri, with offerings of food and drink and the raising of a ceremonial serge (post) for blessing and protection.

sources.reference: Buryat tailgan ritual tradition; Abai Geser epic cult

attributes.name: Horned helmet of the storm-king
attributes.notes: Conical helmet adorned with bull's horns, sign of strength and fertility, worn in the smiting pose with raised mace and forked-lightning spear.

sources.reference: Baal au foudre stele, Ugarit (Louvre AO 15775)

sacredAnimals.name: Bull
sacredAnimals.notes: His chief sacred animal and symbol of virility; he is called 'Bull of Ugarit' and crowned with bull horns.

sources.reference: Baal/Hadad bull iconography; epithet 'Bull of Ugarit'

attributes.name: Bull-horned crown of the enthroned elder
attributes.notes: Depicted as a bearded, seated patriarch in a plumed/horned headdress, mantle and strapped sandals (the gilt bronze El figurine from Ugarit), bull horns marking his epithet 'Bull El'.

sources.reference: Enthroned gilt-bronze 'El' figurine, Ugarit (Negbi, Canaanite Gods in Metal)

sacredAnimals.name: Bull
sacredAnimals.notes: The bull, sign of his strength and creative force, attaches to his title ṯr ʾil, 'Bull El'.

sources.reference: Ugaritic texts, epithet ṯr ʾil ('Bull El')

attributes.name: Armed maiden with sword and bow
attributes.notes: Shown bearing weapons, often winged, as huntress armed with bow and sword, and as a 'Mistress of Animals' grasping or flanked by beasts.

sources.reference: Cornelius, 'Anat and Qudshu as Mistress of Animals'; Levantine Anat iconography

sacredAnimals.name: Lion
sacredAnimals.notes: The lion is her companion and sacred beast in Phoenician depictions of the warrior-huntress.

sources.reference: Phoenician Anat iconography; Mistress of Animals motif

sacredAnimals.name: Lion
sacredAnimals.notes: The chief goddess (Qudshu/Asherah) stands upon a lion in Levantine and Egyptianizing iconography.

sources.reference: Qudshu/Asherah iconography; Hestrin, 'Understanding Asherah' (BAR 1991)

sacredPlants.name: Sacred tree / date palm
sacredPlants.notes: Associated with the stylised sacred tree and date palm, and with the consecrated 'asherah' pole that represents the living tree of the mother-goddess.

sources.reference: Asherah / asherah-pole tradition; sacred-tree iconography

sacredAnimals.name: Lion
sacredAnimals.notes: Lion of war and power, shown as warrior-huntress mastering lions.

sources.reference: Astarte/Athtart iconography (lion, horse, dove, star of Venus)

sacredAnimals.name: Horse
sacredAnimals.notes: Astarte rides or drives horses and chariots, emblem of her martial aspect.

sources.reference: Astarte/Athtart iconography

sacredAnimals.name: Dove
sacredAnimals.notes: Dove of love and beauty, her symbol alongside the eight-pointed star of the planet Venus.

sources.reference: Astarte/Athtart iconography; identification with Venus

sacredAnimals.name: Snow lion
sacredAnimals.notes: In Tibetan painting the guardian-king of the north is mounted on a snow lion while bearing the victory banner and jewel-spitting mongoose.

sources.reference: Tibetan Vaiśravaṇa iconography

sacredAnimals.name: Jewel-spitting mongoose
sacredAnimals.notes: The mongoose (nakula) that vomits jewels, sign of generosity that conquers the snakes of greed and of his wealth-giving power.

sources.reference: Bishamonten/Tamonten iconographic tradition

attributes.name: Red king with stūpa and serpent
attributes.notes: Red-faced king holding a stūpa in one hand and a nāga (serpent) in the other; he gazes at the stūpa to avert his harmful glance.

sources.reference: Four Heavenly Kings (Lokapāla) iconographic tradition

sacredAnimals.name: Nāga (serpent-dragon)
sacredAnimals.notes: Lord of the nāgas; the serpent he holds is emblematic of rain and agricultural fertility.

sources.reference: Four Heavenly Kings (Lokapāla) iconographic tradition

attributes.name: Blue-faced king with sword
attributes.notes: Armoured guardian of the south with a blue face, brandishing his sword of wisdom that cuts ignorance.

sources.reference: Four Heavenly Kings (Lokapāla) iconographic tradition; Cleveland Museum of Art 1918.544

attributes.name: White conch and yak-tail fly-whisk
attributes.notes: Holds a conch shell in one hand and a yak-tail fly-whisk in the other as celestial king of the nats.

sources.reference: Thagyamin iconographic tradition, Burma

attributes.name: Golden book and dog-skin book
attributes.notes: The two books in which he records, at the new year, the deeds of the virtuous (gold) and the wicked (dog-skin leather).

sources.reference: Thagyamin / Thingyan tradition, Burma

sacredAnimals.name: Three-headed white elephant (Airāvata / Erawan)
sacredAnimals.notes: Rides the three-headed white elephant Airāvaṇa when descending to the human world.

sources.reference: Thagyamin / Airāvata (Erawan) tradition

attributes.name: Dressed coconut on the house-post
attributes.notes: Embodied in a coconut, robed in a red gaung-baung-style cloth, hung on the chief post of the house as the indwelling household guardian.

sources.reference: Mahagiri household-nat tradition, Burma

attributes.name: Warrior who hovers in cloud and rains down arrows
attributes.notes: Imagined hovering above the enemy host hidden in cloud and rain, loosing arrows; depicted by his relics — jawbone, shield, spear and a leopard/lion-skin stool.

sources.reference: Kibuka shrine relics; Roscoe, The Baganda (1911)

attributes.name: Flower-eating mother-spirit of Popa
attributes.notes: Figured among the brightly robed images of the Thirty-Seven Nats at Taungkalat as Popa Medaw, the ogress-mother holding or surrounded by the flowers of the mountain.

sources.reference: Taungkalat shrine of the Thirty-Seven Nats, Mount Popa

sacredPlants.name: Flowers of Mount Popa
sacredPlants.notes: Her food and emblem; Popa itself takes its name from Pali/Skt. puppha, 'flower', and bottled flowers are sold as offerings.

sources.reference: Mount Popa / Popa Medaw tradition

attributes.name: Smith's hammer and tongs
attributes.notes: The divine craftsman of the smithy; closest regional iconographic kin is Egyptian Ptah of Memphis, the bearded patron of craftsmen with the smith's tools, with whom Kothar's Memphis abode (ḥkpt) identifies him. Greek heir is Hephaestus with hammer and tongs.

sources.reference: Kothar–Ptah identification (ḥkpt = Hut-ka-Ptah); Smith, Ugaritic Baal Cycle
